title: Convergent World Representations and Divergent Tasks
claim: Separating the underlying world, the data-generating tasks and the trained model into three stages gives a controlled setup for studying representation geometry and adaptation.
layout: 3 stacked rounded panels, top-to-bottom; world, tasks, model; training plot with PCA insets
description: The figure has three stacked, rounded-border panels labeled WORLD, DATA GENERATION PROCESS and MODEL. WORLD (blue border) shows two scatter maps of city coordinates colored by region. A red 'Update' arrow links them, and the right map adds a circled red 'Atlantis' cluster. DATA GENERATION PROCESS (black border) shows seven small geometric sketches with formulas: distance, triangle area, angle, compass direction, inside-triangle, perimeter and line-crossing. MODEL (bottom) shows training curves of cross-entropy for train and validation, with angle error and position error beneath. 3D PCA scatter insets branch off the curves at different training steps, with lines pointing to them. At right, a purple question asks whether new entities are integrated through fine-tuning. A final colored map marks Atlantis in red.
caption: Overview of the World-Data-Model framework. Top: The world consists of 5,075 real city coordinates; we test adaptation by adding 100 synthetic Atlantis cities (App. [ref]). Middle: Seven geometric tasks generate training data from city coordinates (App. [ref]). Bottom: Training dynamics of one model, showing loss curves, linear probing accuracy for coordinate reconstruction and visualizations of internal representations (PCA and linear probe projections) at different training stages. See App. Fig. [ref] for all training curves.
abstract: While neural representations are central to modern deep learning, the conditions governing their geometry and their roles in downstream adaptability remain poorly understood. We develop a framework clearly separating the underlying world, the data generation process and the resulting model representations to study these questions in a controlled setup. 5,075 city coordinates define the world and 7 geometric tasks generate the training data for autoregressive training. We find that different tasks give rise to qualitatively and quantitatively distinct world representation geometries. However, multi-task training drives convergence of world representations: models trained on non-overlapping tasks develop aligned geometric representations, providing controlled evidence for the Multitask Scaling Hypothesis of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. To study adaptation, we pretrain models on all tasks, then test whether new entities (cities) can be consistently integrated into the representation space via fine-tuning. Surprisingly, we find that despite multi-task pretraining, some tasks, which we call divergent, actively harm the representational integration of new entities and harm generalization. Our results show that training on multiple relational tasks reliably produces convergent world representations, but lurking divergent tasks can catastrophically harm new entity integration via fine-tuning.
